# Verification Planning {#sec-ch02}

> The plan is the only verification document the design team will read.

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
After this chapter you will be able to:

1. Decompose a specification into features, including the requirements it never marked as requirements.
2. Write a plan item with a stimulus intent, a checking intent, a coverage intent and a closure criterion.
3. Distinguish code coverage from functional coverage and say what each one proves.
4. Define sign-off criteria before any RTL exists, and explain why a goal set afterwards is not a goal.
5. Keep a plan as a machine-readable file that the regression reports against, and read its report.
:::

## The plan nobody read

Every verification team has a plan. The question is when it was written and whether anything reads it.

The failure has a recognizable shape. The testbench is built first, because the RTL is arriving and something has to run. Tests accumulate, each one written for the feature that happened to be on the designer's desk that week. Months in, a manager asks for the verification plan, and one is produced: a spreadsheet listing the tests that exist, with a column that says which feature each one covers. The coverage goal is set to a round number a little above where coverage already stands. Everyone is relieved. The document describes the past and calls it the future.

Practitioners have been describing this for decades. A 2013 industry paper on planning practice put it plainly: some engineers "would like to treat verification planning as an afterthought if it is done at all", and the result is "little to no consistency among verification documentation" [@ehlers2013planning]. The same paper names the other half of the failure, the plan that was written on time and then abandoned: late design changes "can often invalidate a large portion of work already done in the verification planning process", and nobody goes back. The industry's longest-running survey of verification practice reports, edition after edition, that design errors are the leading cause of functional flaws and that "problems associated with changing, incorrect, and incomplete specifications are a common theme" [@foster2022wrg]. A plan that is not connected to the specification cannot notice when the specification changes.

Even disciplined projects show the scars. OpenTitan, an open-source silicon project whose verification methodology this chapter uses as its primary example precisely because everything about it is public, keeps a machine-readable plan for every block. Its UART plan lists twenty test points in detail. Its coverage section contains a single placeholder covergroup, named `foo_cg`, with an empty description [@opentitan-uart-testplan]. Someone meant to come back.

This chapter is about the alternative: a plan written before the tests, from the specification rather than from the RTL, executed by machines rather than transcribed by people, and read, above all, by the design team, because it is the most precise statement anyone will make about what their design is supposed to do. The chapter ends by giving the FIFO from @sec-ch01 the plan it never had, and by letting a small program read that plan and report, honestly, that the FIFO is not done.

## What a verification plan is {#sec-ch02-what}

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A **verification plan** is the list of every behavior the design must have, each paired with how that behavior will be exercised, how it will be checked, how the checking will be measured, and what will count as done. It is written from the specification, before the testbench, and it is the reference against which verification progress is reported.
:::

The definition has more parts than most people expect, and each part exists because of a failure that happens without it. Without "every behavior", the plan is a list of tests, and features nobody thought to test are invisible. Without "how it will be exercised", a feature can be listed and never reached. Without "how it will be checked", a test can reach the feature and not notice it is broken, which is the lesson of @sec-ch01-example. Without "how the checking will be measured", nobody can say whether the test that exists actually did what the plan says. Without "what counts as done", the goal drifts to wherever the project happens to be when the schedule runs out.

The canonical textbooks agree on the outline while differing in emphasis. Bergeron frames the plan as the document that decides, before a testbench exists, what will be verified, by which method, at which level of the design hierarchy, and when the job is finished [@bergeron2003testbenches]. Wile, Goss and Roesner make the plan the first artifact of their verification cycle after the specification itself, and a joint product of the architecture, design and verification teams rather than a verification deliverable [@wile2005cfv]. Piziali's book is about the part of the plan that becomes the coverage model, and its method of deriving coverage top-down from features rather than bottom-up from the RTL is the one this chapter follows [@piziali2004coverage]. The most widely used free treatment, the Verification Academy coverage cookbook, reduces the plan to four questions that every feature must answer: what needs to be tested, under what conditions, what testbench infrastructure is required to drive and monitor it, and how the testbench will check that it works [@va-coverage-cookbook].

Two standards touch the plan without defining its format. IEEE 1012 prescribes the contents of a verification and validation plan for systems, software and hardware at defined integrity levels [@ieee1012-2024]; industry verification plans are looser than its outline, but a project in a safety-critical domain will be asked to show how its plan maps onto that outline. The Unified Coverage Interoperability Standard defines a "verification plan hierarchy" as a data structure that tools can attach coverage results to, and a tag mechanism for linking plan nodes to the coverage and design scopes that satisfy them [@ucis2012]. That is interchange, not authoring: UCIS lets a plan report be produced from any tool's coverage database, but says nothing about how the plan was written.

This book says "verification plan" rather than "test plan" for a reason the definition makes visible. Tests are one column of the plan. A test plan that lists tests and nothing else has already lost the checking and coverage columns, and with them the ability to say what the tests proved.

## From specification to features {#sec-ch02-features}

The plan begins with a reading of the specification that is closer than the designer's. The designer reads the specification to decide how to build the block. The verification engineer reads it to enumerate everything the block must do, and, just as importantly, everything the specification does not say.

### The reading discipline

Every sentence containing "shall", "must" or "will" is a requirement. So is every table, every timing diagram, every register field description, and most sentences containing "when" or "if". Specifications rarely mark their requirements. The UART specification provided for this chapter's exercises has a sentence that reads "Writing DATA while TX_FULL is set is ignored." Nothing marks it as a requirement. It is one, it is testable, and a testbench that does not know about it will never try the write.

The cookbook's advice is to compile the requirements *before* planning starts and to classify each as a rule, which is mandatory, or a suggestion, which is not [@va-coverage-cookbook]. The distinction matters at sign-off: a rule that is not verified blocks tapeout; a suggestion that is not verified is a documented risk.

The hardest case is the feature that has no description at all. The 2013 planning paper identifies it as "an undefined design component or design feature which has no documented description and requires a significant amount of research and effort on the part of the verification engineer to develop a meaningful verification plan" [@ehlers2013planning]. Such features are found by asking the designer, and the answers belong in the specification, not in the plan. OpenTitan's methodology makes the same point from the review side: the plan review's feedback "flows both ways", and "the language in the design specification could be made more precise, and missing items in both the design specification and the testplan can be identified and added" [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. Planning is the first, cheapest specification review a design gets.

### Decomposition axes

A feature list produced by reading alone is only as complete as the reader's attention. A set of decomposition axes catches what reading misses. Six work for almost any block:

1. **Interfaces.** Each port or bus, its protocol rules, and its behavior under back-pressure, idle and reset.
2. **Protocol rules.** Every ordering, handshake and timing constraint the interface specification imposes.
3. **Registers and fields.** Every register, every field, its reset value, access type and side effects on read or write.
4. **Modes and configurations.** Every parameter, every control bit, and the combinations that are legal.
5. **Error and corner conditions.** Every "shall be ignored", "is not allowed" and "produces undefined results"; every boundary of every counter and queue.
6. **Performance.** Throughput, latency and any "within N cycles" the specification promises.

OpenTitan encodes a version of this in its naming convention: a plan item's name is a lower-snake-case path from main feature to sub-feature, so that the plan's structure mirrors the specification's [@opentitan-testplanner]. It also factors the axes that every block shares, register access, interrupts, alerts and bus protocol, into shared plan fragments that each block's plan imports rather than rewrites [@opentitan-testplanner]. A verification team that has done this once has a template for every block that follows.

### The FIFO's features

The FIFO in @sec-ch01-example came with a four-sentence contract in its header comment. Read with the discipline above, those four sentences and the module's parameters yield about a dozen features. Reset behavior. Write, read, and their ordering. The full and empty flags, each with its "and only then" clause, which is a separate requirement from the flag itself. A write while full and a read while empty, both "shall be ignored", which are the corner conditions the contract mentions and the directed test in @sec-ch01 never tried. A simultaneous read and write, which the contract does not mention at all and which the reader must ask the designer about. The parameters, which imply a configuration axis. And a property the contract implies but never states: occupancy shall never exceed the depth. The plan file in @sec-ch02-example lists all twelve.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
A feature describes what the design must do, not how the design does it. "The full flag shall be asserted when all sixteen entries are occupied" is a feature. "The full flag shall be asserted when `count == 15`" is the implementation, and a plan item written that way would have verified the bug in @sec-ch01-example as correct behavior. Features are written from the specification, with the RTL closed.
:::

## From features to plan items {#sec-ch02-items}

A feature becomes a plan item when it is paired with the evidence that will verify it. The anatomy of an item is the same in a spreadsheet, a requirements-management tool or OpenTitan's Hjson, and the names vary less than one might expect.

- **Identifier.** Stable across specification revisions, so that a test or a coverage group can name it and the link survives.
- **Feature and requirement.** The behavior, in the specification's words.
- **Stimulus intent.** What must be driven for the behavior to occur. Not a test, but what a test must do.
- **Checking intent.** What must be observed and compared, and against what reference. This is the column that turns a test into evidence, and it is the one most often left blank.
- **Coverage intent.** What must be measured to prove the stimulus reached the behavior: which values, states or crosses.
- **Closure criterion.** What "done" means for this item: which tests must pass, which coverage points must be hit, or which property must be proven.
- **Priority and stage.** Must-have or should-have; and, on a staged project, which milestone the item belongs to.
- **Owner.**

OpenTitan's schema has the same shape with fewer words. Each test point has a name, a stage, a description whose recommended template is a goal, a stimulus and a check, and a list of tests that "is initially empty" and "gradually updated as tests are written" [@opentitan-testplanner]. That last phrase is the whole philosophy in one field: the plan exists before the tests, and the tests fill it in.

Three kinds of item deserve separate mention. **Directed items** describe a specific scenario the specification calls out by name, and are verified by a test written for that scenario. **Random items** describe a behavior that must hold across a space of conditions, and are verified by constrained-random stimulus with a checker, the pattern of @sec-ch01-example; their coverage intent is what makes the space explicit. **Negative items** describe what must never happen: no overflow, no lost transaction, no deadlock. Simulation can only show that a negative item held for the cycles it ran. Formal verification, which Part IV covers, can prove one, and a plan should say which method each negative item expects.

### Traceability

The chain from requirement to result is the plan's reason to exist, and in regulated domains it is a formal obligation. A 2024 industry paper from a mixed-signal company states the requirement in a form worth adopting verbatim: "Requirements shall be traceable through the verification plan to regression results, which shall be demonstrable and visible to all members of the development team" [@kreisinger2024traceability]. The same paper describes the mechanism that keeps the chain honest when the specification changes: every link downstream of a changed requirement is marked *suspect* until someone re-examines it, and "having a verification plan clear of suspect relationships is a necessary condition for verification closure" [@kreisinger2024traceability].

![The traceability chain. A requirement in the specification becomes a feature, the feature becomes a plan item, the item names its tests and coverage, and the regression reports results back against the item. A change anywhere upstream makes every link downstream suspect until re-examined.](../figures/ch02-traceability.svg){#fig-ch02-traceability fig-alt="Chain of boxes: specification requirement, feature, plan item, tests and coverage, regression results, with a feedback arrow marking downstream links suspect after a change."}

The automotive functional-safety standard ISO 26262 requires a documented verification plan and bidirectional traceability between safety requirements and verification evidence, with rigor scaled by the automotive safety integrity level [@iso26262-2018]. The airborne-hardware guidance DO-254 is requirements-based throughout: every requirement traces to a verification activity and a result, and for the highest design-assurance levels an elemental analysis, in practice code coverage, is expected as well [@do254-2000]. Both descriptions are summaries; a project in either domain reads the standard's own clauses. The point for this chapter is that the plan item, with its identifier and its named tests and coverage, is the unit of traceability in every one of these regimes.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
The plan review is the most valuable meeting in a verification project, and its most valuable output is disagreement. OpenTitan reviews the plan "face-to-face" with the designers, verification peers, leads and the teams that will integrate the block [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. When a designer says "that's not what the spec means", one of three things is true: the plan is wrong, the specification is ambiguous, or the design is about to be wrong. All three are cheaper to discover in the meeting than in silicon.
:::

## The coverage model, designed from the plan {#sec-ch02-coverage}

Coverage is how a plan item's "how will we measure it" column is answered, and it comes in two kinds that prove different things.

### Code coverage

Code coverage is measured by the simulator without being asked. Line coverage records which statements executed. Toggle coverage records which signals changed value in both directions. Branch and condition coverage record which arms of each `if` and `case`, and which terms of each condition, were taken. State-machine coverage records which states and transitions were visited. Assertion coverage records which assertions were evaluated and which passed.

All of these prove one thing: that the simulation reached a place in the code. None of them proves that anything was checked when it got there. A testbench with no checker at all can reach 100 percent line coverage. Code coverage's value is the opposite direction: a line that was never executed is a behavior that was never verified, whatever the plan says. OpenTitan collects line, toggle, state-machine, condition, branch and assertion coverage, restricts toggle coverage to the block's and its sub-modules' ports because internal toggles are too many to be meaningful, and treats already-verified sub-modules as black boxes [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. Those are practical decisions every project makes, and the plan is where they are recorded.

### Functional coverage

Functional coverage is written by a person, from the plan. OpenTitan's definition is as good as any: explicit, manually created points that capture "whether signals (that reflect the current state of the design) have met an interesting set or a sequence of values" [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. A *cover point* names a signal or expression and the *bins* of values that matter. A *cross* records combinations of cover points. The constructs are SystemVerilog covergroups and the assertion-coverage directives that Part II teaches; what this chapter cares about is where they come from.

They come from the plan's coverage-intent column, and OpenTitan's plan format makes that concrete by keeping the planned covergroups in the plan file, each with a name and a description of the points and crosses it should contain. One of its examples describes a timer block's covergroup as covering the combinations of inputs that produce a timeout, the ranges of the step and prescaler values as bucketed cover points, and their cross [@opentitan-testplanner]. The plan says what the covergroup must contain before anyone writes the covergroup. OpenTitan's methodology states the two-part structure directly: a test plan that lists the tests planned to verify each feature, and a functional coverage plan that lists the cover points and crosses needed to prove the tests did so [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. Piziali's method for deriving the points, identifying each feature's attributes and the values of each attribute that matter, then choosing which combinations to cross, is the systematic version of the same idea [@piziali2004coverage].

### Goals, holes and waivers

A coverage goal is a statement about the coverage model, not about the design. "100 percent functional coverage" means every bin the plan asked for was hit. If the plan asked for the wrong bins, the number is meaningless, which is why the coverage model is reviewed as part of the plan. OpenTitan sets its goals by stage: 90 percent code and functional coverage at the stage where all features are exercised, and 100 percent "with waivers" at sign-off [@opentitan-dev-stages].

A hole is a bin that was never hit. Every hole is one of three things: a stimulus gap, meaning the tests never drove the design there and a test is missing; a specification error, meaning the bin describes something that cannot happen; or a coverage-model error, meaning the bin should never have been written. Only the first is fixed with a test. The other two are fixed with a waiver, and a waiver is a documented decision, not a checkbox. OpenTitan requires every exclusion to carry an annotation stating its reason from a fixed vocabulary, unreachable, simulation-only, unsupported feature, covered elsewhere, or low-risk and prohibitively difficult, and requires designers to approve exclusions in code review [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. That vocabulary is worth stealing. A waiver whose reason is not one of those five is usually a hole someone got tired of.

## Sign-off criteria, written before the first test {#sec-ch02-signoff}

@sec-ch01-lifecycle listed what sign-off comprises: coverage closure against the plan, regression health, bug convergence, open-issue review, and reviewed waivers. This section makes each concrete, using OpenTitan's published stages and checklist as an example of a project that wrote its criteria down in public and holds every block to them.

OpenTitan defines four verification stages. At V0 the testbench is being built, the plan is being written, and the method, simulation, formal or both, has been decided. At V1 the environment runs, with documentation and smoke tests. At V2 every interface is connected and exercised, every assertion is written and enabled, and code and functional coverage each reach 90 percent. At V3 every bug is addressed, every test passes with every seed, and coverage reaches 100 percent with documented waivers [@opentitan-dev-stages]. Each stage has a checklist of named items that must be signed off before the block advances. The plan appears in the first stage's list, as an item requiring a completed machine-readable plan with test points mapped to features and a functional coverage plan, and again as a review item [@opentitan-checklist].

Three of the checklist's later items make the sign-off criteria of @sec-ch01 exact:

- **Regression health.** At V2, the nightly regression must be 90 percent passing; at V3, 100 percent passing with a soak of at least one week [@opentitan-checklist]. Each random test runs with many seeds, one hundred by the project's own stated convention, because a test that passes with one seed has been run once [@opentitan-dv-methodology].
- **Coverage closure.** Code coverage of every kind and functional coverage at 90 percent for V2 and 100 percent for V3, with the waiver rules of @sec-ch02-coverage [@opentitan-checklist].
- **Open issues.** No high-priority issues pending at V2, every low-priority issue root-caused, and no issues pending at all at V3 [@opentitan-checklist].

Two criteria from @sec-ch01 do not appear as numbers. Bug convergence, the observation that the rate of new bugs has fallen toward zero, is universal practice and appears in the textbooks, but no public project the research behind this chapter could find states it as a threshold; it is a judgment made in the sign-off review with the bug-rate curve on the table. And the traceability condition from @sec-ch02-items, that no link in the chain is suspect, is stated by the paper that introduced the term as a necessary condition for closure [@kreisinger2024traceability].

Why do the criteria belong in the plan, written at V0? Because a goal chosen after the fact is a description. OpenTitan chose 90 and 100 percent, one hundred seeds and a one-week soak before any block existed, and every block is measured against the same numbers. A project that sets its coverage goal in the last month sets it to what it has.

## The living plan {#sec-ch02-living}

A plan that lives in a document is dead within a month, because nothing updates it. A plan that lives in a file the regression reads is updated every night.

The medium matters less than the property. The 2013 planning paper is explicit that a spreadsheet is fine, provided the plan template is built in whatever tool the team will actually use [@ehlers2013planning]. The cookbook's executable test plan is a spreadsheet or XML document that the coverage tool reads and annotates with results [@va-coverage-cookbook]. The commercial planning tools from the three major vendors each offer a plan editor linked to regression and coverage databases, with traceability to requirements as their selling point [@cadence-verisium-manager; @synopsys-verdi-vms; @siemens-questa-vm]; the mixed-signal company's paper cited above keeps its plan inside a requirements-management tool and links it to one of those regression managers [@kreisinger2024traceability]. UCIS is the standard that lets coverage results move between such tools with their plan attachments intact [@ucis2012].

OpenTitan's version is the simplest to understand because all of it is visible. The plan is a text file in a human-writable, machine-parseable format, kept in the repository next to the RTL. A tool reads it and inserts the plan and coverage plan as tables into the block's verification document, so that the document is generated from the plan rather than maintained alongside it. The same tool joins the plan's test names with the nightly regression's results, keyed by test name, and produces a per-item table of passing and total runs and a per-stage progress figure, linked to the coverage dashboard [@opentitan-dv-methodology]. Nobody transcribes anything. When a test is added, its name goes into one plan item's test list, and the next night's report includes it.

That join, plan item to test name to result, is the entire mechanism of a living plan, and it needs no vendor tool. The worked example that follows implements it in a hundred lines of Python.

::: {.callout-important title="Future Directions"}
Generating the feature list and the plan from the specification is an obvious target for language models, and the measured results are instructive. A 2026 study from a processor vendor's research group separated plan generation from testbench execution and found that frontier models' generated test plans passed a known-good design only 15.7 to 21.7 percent of the time; a model fine-tuned for the task reached 33.3 percent, and detected deliberately introduced bugs 13.9 percent of the time [@kochar2026grpo]. An industry paper on formal test-plan generation reports at least 80 percent accuracy on three designs, assessed by the authors against their own reference plans [@jain2024genai-fv-testplan]. Vendor announcements report an unnamed customer producing a plan in under forty minutes against a week by hand [@eetimes2026chipstack]; that is a claim supplied through a press release, not a measurement. The pattern is the one Part VII returns to: drafting is fast, and the plan review of @sec-ch02-items, which decides whether the draft describes the specification, is still a person's job.
:::

## Worked example: a plan for the FIFO {#sec-ch02-example}

The FIFO of @sec-ch01-example was verified by two tests and no plan. This section writes the plan it should have had, then lets a small tool read the plan and the book's own example records and report what the evidence supports.

### The plan file

The plan is a YAML file, chosen for readability; its structure is the same as OpenTitan's Hjson test plans, with the checking and closure columns made explicit. Each of the twelve items pairs a requirement, in the contract's words, with a stimulus intent, a checking intent, a coverage intent, a closure criterion, a priority and the tests that provide its evidence. The header comment states the one rule that makes the report honest: an item lists only the tests that can vouch for it.

```{.yaml include="examples/ch02-verification-planning/plan/fifo_plan.yaml"}
```

Read the tests columns. Items 001 to 003, reset, write and read, list the directed test from @sec-ch01, which exercises exactly those behaviors at low occupancy. Items 004 to 006 and 009, ordering, the two flags and simultaneous access, list the random test, because only random traffic reaches the occupancies where those behaviors matter. Items 007 and 008, the two "shall be ignored" corners, list nothing: no test in @sec-ch01 ever attempted a write while full or a read while empty. Item 010, the no-overflow property, lists nothing because it wants a proof, not a test. Items 011 and 012 are should-haves with no evidence yet.

### The report tool

The tool reads the plan and the status file that the book's example checker writes (@sec-appF-checking), and classifies every item.

```{.python include="examples/ch02-verification-planning/plan/plan_report.py"}
```

One function deserves attention. The status file records whether each *example* behaved as expected, and some of the book's examples are expected to fail because they exist to expose a bug. The plan does not care about examples; it cares about the design. So the tool inverts the expectation: an example marked as expected to fail, which failed as expected, is evidence that the design *failed* that item. Without that inversion the report would have declared the full-flag requirement verified by a test that proved it broken.

### The report

```{.text include="examples/ch02-verification-planning/plan/run.out"}
```

Read it against the plan. Three items pass: reset, write and read, on the strength of the directed test. Four items fail: ordering, both flags and simultaneous access, all of them backed by the random test, which stopped at the first error. The first error was item 005, the full flag asserted one entry early, which is the bug from @sec-ch01-example; the other three are marked failing not because they are known to be broken but because the test that was supposed to prove them did not finish, and a test that did not finish proves nothing. Five items have no evidence at all, three of them must-haves. The tool's last line refuses to call the FIFO done and names the items that stand in the way, and its exit status carries the same verdict to whatever called it, which is how a plan report becomes a gate in a regression rather than a document in a folder.

The report told the team three things the two tests could not. It said which requirements the passing test actually covered, which was fewer than the test's author assumed. It said which requirements had never been tried, and the two "shall be ignored" corners are precisely the kind of requirement a designer's own tests skip. And it said what closing would take: fix the bug, re-run the random test, write two corner-case tests, prove one property, and decide whether the two should-have items are in scope. That is a plan.

## Summary

- A verification plan pairs every required behavior with how it will be exercised, checked, measured and closed. It is written from the specification, before the testbench, and reported against by the regression.
- Features are extracted by reading every sentence as a possible requirement and by sweeping six axes: interfaces, protocol rules, registers, modes, corner conditions and performance. Features describe what the design must do, never how it does it.
- A plan item's checking intent is the column most often left blank and the one that turns a test into evidence. Negative items should say whether they expect a proof.
- Traceability from requirement to result is the plan's purpose, a formal obligation in regulated domains, and kept honest by marking downstream links suspect when anything upstream changes.
- Code coverage proves a line ran; functional coverage proves a planned behavior occurred. Both are designed from the plan, and a coverage goal is a statement about the model, not the design.
- Holes are stimulus gaps, specification errors or model errors. Only the first is fixed with a test; the others need a documented, reviewed waiver with a stated reason.
- Sign-off criteria are numbers and conditions chosen before the first test and applied to every block. A goal set afterwards describes the present.
- A living plan is a machine-readable file whose items name their tests, so that the regression's results join to the plan by name and the report is generated, not maintained.

## Exercises

1. Take the UART specification in `examples/ch02-verification-planning/uart-spec/` and produce a feature list using the six decomposition axes. Count the requirements you found that the specification did not mark as such. There are more than ten.
2. Write plan items, in the format of the FIFO plan, for three of those features, one of which must be a negative feature. State the closure criterion for each and say which method, simulation or formal, each expects.
3. For the FIFO plan, identify every item better proved by formal verification than by simulation, and for each say what a simulation-based closure criterion would leave unproven.
4. Write a test for item FIFO-007 (a write while full), add its directory to the item's test list, re-run the example checker for the chapter and then the report tool. Explain what changed in the report and what did not, and why item 005 still fails.
5. The specification changes: the FIFO gains a programmable almost-full threshold register. Update the plan, then list every downstream artifact, in the plan and outside it, that the change makes suspect.
6. Choose one test point in OpenTitan's public HMAC test plan [@opentitan-hmac-testplan], and trace it to the test that implements it and the covergroup that measures it in the repository. Record how long the trace took and what you needed to know to make it.
7. The FIFO plan's coverage intents describe bins in prose. Rewrite item 005's coverage intent as an explicit list of bins and one cross, in the style of OpenTitan's covergroup descriptions, without writing any SystemVerilog.

## Further reading

- Janick Bergeron, *Writing Testbenches: Functional Verification of HDL Models*, 2nd ed. [@bergeron2003testbenches]. Its verification-plan chapter is the origin of the feature-first, priority-ordered plan.
- Bruce Wile, John Goss and Wolfgang Roesner, *Comprehensive Functional Verification* [@wile2005cfv]. Places the plan in the full verification cycle.
- Andrew Piziali, *Functional Verification Coverage Measurement and Analysis* [@piziali2004coverage]. The method for deriving a coverage model from features.
- Siemens Verification Academy, *Coverage Cookbook* [@va-coverage-cookbook]. The specification-to-test-plan and test-plan-to-coverage chapters.
- OpenTitan project, DV methodology [@opentitan-dv-methodology], test plan format [@opentitan-testplanner], development stages [@opentitan-dev-stages] and sign-off checklist [@opentitan-checklist]. A complete, public, working instance of everything in this chapter.
- Ehlers, Vargas and Carzola, "Best Practices in Verification Planning" [@ehlers2013planning], and Kreisinger and Chatterjee, "Verification Plan in Requirements Management Tool" [@kreisinger2024traceability]. Two practitioner accounts, eleven years apart, of the same discipline.
